analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers charge older adults up to five times more than young adults for insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died at the end of the 115th Congress with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change an Obamacare rule that limits how much more insurers can charge older adults than young adults for the same policy. Today that gap is capped at 3 to 1; the bill would raise the cap to 5 to 1 starting in 2018, or let each state set its own cap with no federal limit at all [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Young, healthy adults buying their own coverage would likely see lower premiums, since insurers could shift more of the bill onto older enrollees. Health insurers would gain pricing flexibility they sought, including the option to charge older customers far more in states that allow it. States would also gain authority to set their own age-rating ratio [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Young adults buying individual coverage would likely pay lower premiums, because raising the allowed ratio from 3 to 1 to 5 to 1 lets insurers shift more of the cost onto older enrollees.
States would gain the power to set their own age-rating ratio rather than live under the federal 3-to-1 cap, giving them latitude to redesign their individual markets.
Insurers would gain wider pricing flexibility, which supporters argued could help them price plans attractively for younger customers and stabilize the individual market.

analysis.who_pays: Adults roughly 50 to 64 who buy their own insurance — most of them working people not yet on Medicare — would face substantially higher premiums, since a 5-to-1 cap (or a state-set ratio with no cap) lets insurers charge them up to 67% more relative to young adults than the current 3-to-1 rule allows. The bill also weakens a uniform federal protection by letting states set any ratio they choose [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Older adults buying their own coverage

drawbacks.text: Adults in their 50s and early 60s would pay sharply higher premiums: moving from a 3-to-1 to a 5-to-1 ratio allows insurers to charge a 64-year-old up to 67% more relative to a young adult than under current law, which could push many older working people to drop coverage.

The federal floor disappears entirely at the state level: the bill lets a state set 'such other ratio... as the State involved may provide,' meaning a state could allow unlimited age-based pricing, not just 5 to 1.

If higher premiums drive older, less healthy people out of the individual market, the remaining pool gets sicker and more expensive, which can raise costs for everyone still insured — a risk critics of looser age rating have long raised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straight redistribution within the insurance market: whatever young buyers save, older buyers pay, and the insurer gets discretion over the split. It offers real help to young adults struggling with premiums, but that help is paid for almost entirely by people in their 50s and early 60s — often older workers earning modest incomes, not the wealthy. The open-ended state option goes further than the advertised 5-to-1 change, since a state could remove the cap altogether. Because the bill never advanced, its actual costs and benefits were never debated on the floor or scored in detail.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup and no vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Larry Bucshon introduced the bill on January 27, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On February 3, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill attracted only 2 cosponsors, both Republicans, and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Adults in their 50s and early 60s who buy their own insurance kept the existing 3-to-1 cap on age-based premiums, and insurers did not gain the looser pricing rules they wanted. Young adults gained nothing, but also lost nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Older adults kept the 3-to-1 premium cap

for.name: 2 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on February 3, 2017, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the record shows no further action

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll call shows the split; the bill's only three supporters — the sponsor and 2 cosponsors — were all Republicans, and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The bill gives insurers wider freedom to set premiums by age — up to 5-to-1 federally, or any ratio a state allows — which the industry had sought as flexibility under the ACA. Insurers benefit regardless of who wins the resulting cost shift; older enrollees would pay the difference.

Not an industry but the group bearing the bill's direct cost: loosening the 3-to-1 cap lets insurers price their policies substantially higher relative to young adults, and the state option could remove the cap entirely.
